title: Why 5 == 5.0 is True but 5 is 5.0 is False in Python
description:
Python's == and is look almost the same but check completely different things -- one compares values, the other compares object identity. This tiny gotcha trips up a lot of new Python developers, especially once you start comparing things to None. Full lesson on variables, types, and operators is linked below.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/02-variables-data-types/

#Shorts

beats.narration: In Python, five equals five point zero comes back true. But five is five point zero comes back false. Same value. Totally different answer.

Here's why. Double equals checks if the values match -- and five and five point zero are equal in value. But 'is' checks identity, whether they're literally the same object in memory. An int and a float are never the same object.

display.code:
print(5 == 5.0)       # True (value equality)
print(5 is 5.0)       # False (different objects/types)

beats.narration: Rule of thumb: use double equals to compare values, and save 'is' for checking if two variables literally point to the same object -- like comparing to None.
